title: World Religions and Ethics
summary: Learn about the world's major religious traditions, including African traditional religions, Judaism, Christianity, Islam, Hinduism, Buddhism and Sikhism, and the main approaches to ethics, applied ethics and respectful dialogue.
audience: Students, teachers, community leaders and anyone interested in beliefs and values

body.p: Religion shapes the lives of most people in the world, influencing values, family life, art, politics and community. Studying religions academically means describing beliefs and practices accurately and fairly, as their followers understand them, without promoting or attacking any faith. Within every religion there is great diversity of belief and practice.

list: Beliefs: teachings about God or gods, the world, humanity, life after death.
Practices: worship, prayer, rituals, festivals, rites of passage.
Community and institutions: congregations, leaders, schools and charities.
Ethics: teachings on how to live.
History and change: how traditions developed and spread.

body.p: Worldwide, Christianity and Islam are the largest religions, together followed by more than half of humanity; Hinduism, Buddhism, Judaism, Sikhism, traditional and folk religions and other faiths have many followers, and a large number of people are not religiously affiliated. Africa is home to large Christian and Muslim populations as well as living African traditional religions.

body.tip: Use the terms and names followers use for themselves, and avoid treating one tradition as the standard by which others are judged.

body.p: African traditional religions are the indigenous religious traditions of the continent's many peoples. They vary widely, but often share some features:

list: Belief in a supreme creator God, known by many names, such as Olodumare among the Yoruba, Ngai among the Kikuyu and uMvelinqangi among the Zulu.
Lesser divinities or spirits associated with natural forces or places.
The importance of ancestors, who remain part of the community and are honoured through rituals.
Ritual specialists such as diviners, healers and priests.
Rites of passage marking birth, initiation, marriage and death.
A strong link between religion, community, land and morality.

body.p: These traditions are passed on mainly through oral teaching, rituals, proverbs, songs and community practice. Many Africans combine elements of traditional belief with Christianity or Islam. Ideas such as ubuntu, the understanding that "a person is a person through other people", express a widely shared ethical vision of community and mutual responsibility.

body.tip: Avoid outdated terms such as "primitive" or "pagan"; they reflect colonial prejudice rather than understanding.

body.p: Judaism, Christianity and Islam are monotheistic religions that trace their roots to Abraham.

Judaism centres on the covenant between God and the Jewish people, the Torah and the wider Hebrew Bible, observance of commandments, the Sabbath and festivals such as Passover and Yom Kippur. Synagogues are places of prayer and study.

Christians believe in one God as Father, Son and Holy Spirit (the Trinity), and that Jesus Christ is the Son of God whose death and resurrection bring salvation. The Bible includes the Old and New Testaments. Major branches include Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant traditions, with many African independent and Pentecostal churches. Key festivals are Christmas and Easter.

Muslims believe in one God (Allah), with Muhammad as the final prophet, and the Qur'an as God's revealed word. The Five Pillars are the declaration of faith (shahada), prayer five times a day (salat), almsgiving (zakat), fasting during Ramadan (sawm) and pilgrimage to Mecca (hajj) for those able. The main branches are Sunni and Shia. Festivals include Eid al-Fitr and Eid al-Adha.

body.tip: Notice shared figures and values across these traditions, such as Abraham and Moses, alongside their real differences.

lessons.title: Hinduism, Buddhism, Sikhism and other traditions

body.p: Hinduism is a diverse family of traditions originating in South Asia, with sacred texts such as the Vedas, Upanishads and Bhagavad Gita. Key ideas include dharma (duty and right living), karma (actions and their consequences), samsara (the cycle of rebirth) and moksha (liberation). Many deities are worshipped, often understood as forms of one ultimate reality. Diwali is a major festival.

Buddhism follows the teachings of Siddhartha Gautama, the Buddha. The Four Noble Truths describe suffering, its cause (craving), its end and the path to its end, the Noble Eightfold Path, including right understanding, right speech and right mindfulness. Major schools include Theravada and Mahayana.

Sikhism, founded by Guru Nanak in Punjab, teaches belief in one God, equality, honest work and service; the Guru Granth Sahib is its scripture, and the langar (free community kitchen) expresses equality. Other traditions include Jainism, the Baha'i Faith, Confucian and Daoist traditions and many indigenous religions worldwide. Africa has long-established Hindu communities, especially in South Africa and East Africa.

body.tip: Learn one festival from each tradition and what it means to followers; it is a good entry point to understanding.

body.p: Ethics asks how we should live and what makes actions right or wrong. Religious and non-religious thinkers offer several major approaches.

list: Consequentialism (such as utilitarianism): judge actions by their results, aiming for the greatest good for the greatest number.
Deontology (duty ethics): some actions are right or wrong in themselves, whatever the results, such as keeping promises or not lying.
Virtue ethics: focus on character, developing virtues such as honesty, courage, compassion and justice.
Religious ethics: teachings rooted in sacred texts, traditions and communities, such as love of neighbour, justice and mercy.
Ubuntu and communitarian ethics: right action strengthens community, dignity and harmonious relationships.
Human rights: universal rights belonging to every person, expressed in documents such as the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights.

body.p: Each approach has strengths and weaknesses. Consequentialism can seem to justify harming a few for many; strict rules can clash in hard cases. Many people combine approaches.

body.tip: Test your view on a hard case by asking how each approach would judge it; it reveals what you really value.

body.p: Applied ethics uses ethical reasoning on real issues, where religious and secular views may agree or differ: poverty and wealth, care for the environment, medical ethics, business ethics, war and peace, and the treatment of refugees and minorities.

steps: Identify the facts and who is affected.
Identify the values and principles in tension.
Consider the views of different religious and ethical traditions.
Reach a reasoned conclusion, open to further evidence.

body.p: In diverse societies, freedom of religion and belief, including the freedom to have no religion, is protected in many constitutions and international law. Interfaith dialogue brings people of different beliefs together to understand each other and cooperate on shared concerns such as peace-building, health and education. It does not require agreement on beliefs, only respect and honesty.

body.tip: When discussing beliefs, ask questions to understand before you argue; curiosity builds respect.

options: Describing beliefs and practices accurately and fairly
